intro: Thirty meters of reinforced concrete and soapstone stand on Corcovado mountain with arms 28 meters wide. This is how a 1920s design became Brazil's most recognized symbol.
page_title: Christ the Redeemer: Exploded 3D Model and History | Architectural Atlas

sections.body: In the 1920s, Brazil's Catholic community raised funds for a monument on Corcovado mountain, 700 meters above Rio de Janeiro. French sculptor Paul Landowski designed the figure in the Art Deco style then sweeping the world; Brazilian engineer Heitor da Silva Costa engineered it, with French engineer Albert Caquot; Romanian sculptor Gheorghe Leonida fashioned the face. Construction ran from 1922 to 1931. The statue was dedicated on 12 October 1931, the feast of Our Lady Aparecida, patroness of Brazil. Early plans had Christ holding a globe; instead the arms open wide, 28 meters from fingertip to fingertip, as a symbol of peace.
sections.heading: A mountain for a monument

sections.body: The statue is a reinforced concrete core faced with soapstone tiles, chosen for their durability against Rio's tropical weather. It weighs 635 metric tons. The soapstone gives the surface its soft gray luminosity and has protected the concrete for nearly a century, though lightning strikes have required repairs and upgraded protection over the years.
sections.heading: Concrete in soapstone

sections.body: In 2006, on the 75th anniversary of the dedication, the chapel of Nossa Senhora Aparecida inside the pedestal base was consecrated as a shrine, and couples may now marry there. In 2007 the statue was named one of the New Seven Wonders of the World in a global vote, beating New York's Statue of Liberty with the help of millions of Brazilian cell-phone votes. Nearly two million visitors a year now make the trip up Corcovado by rack railway, van, or hiking trail.
sections.heading: A shrine and a wonder

sections.body:
The statue has watched over fictional cities for decades. It appears in Bette Davis's Now Voyager (1942) and Alfred Hitchcock's Notorious (1946), both using Rio as an exotic backdrop. Baz Luhrmann's Romeo + Juliet (1996) sets its Verona Beach under the statue's gaze. The animated Rio (2011) and Fast Five (2011) both feature it in aerial shots of the city, and it appears in The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn, Part 1 (2011).

Its most famous screen moment is its destruction. In the 2009 disaster film 2012, an earthquake topples the statue and it crumbles down the mountainside. Brazilian audiences were offended by the image of their national symbol being destroyed, a reaction widely reported at the time. The statue survives in reality: it has weathered decades of tropical storms and lightning strikes, and still welcomes Rio with open arms.
